subject: RFI: Traffic separation topology, operator guardrails, and trust-zone annotation
messages:
From: Alan Cho <alan.cho@humana.com>

Date: Wed, 22 Apr 2026 09:04:00 -0700
Subject: RFI: Traffic separation topology and trust zones (initial request)

Michael —

Thanks for the quick intro yesterday. As part of Humana's evaluation we need a concise, annotated response on how Redwood separates customer traffic at the network and orchestration layers. The security folks asked for: 1) a high-level network diagram showing control plane / data plane demarcations and operator access paths, 2) an isolation matrix mapping tenant resource types to enforced boundaries and crypto/ACL controls, and 3) a short threat-model summary (top 3 realistic attack paths and how Redwood mitigates them).

If possible please include an operator-facing note on what we do to prevent accidental cross-tenant routing during upgrades (we're particularly concerned about rolling upgrades and KV cache sharing). We don't need source code — a diagram + matrix + one-page narrative will do.

Target timing: would appreciate a draft by EOD today if that's realistic, otherwise tomorrow morning. Thanks — Alan

--
Alan Cho
Sr. Security Engineer, Humana
alan.cho@humana.com
From: michael_grant@redwood.ai <michael_grant@redwood.ai>
To: Alan Cho <alan.cho@humana.com>
Cc: security@humana.com
Date: Wed, 22 Apr 2026 14:10:00 -0700
Subject: Re: RFI: Traffic separation topology and trust zones (initial request)

Alan —

Thanks — we can get a concise packet together. High level update: I'm attaching an annotated topology PDF plus an isolation matrix CSV and a short operator guardrails note. Highlights up front:

- Control plane is hosted in a logically separated management VPC with strict peering and egress controls; customer inference traffic never traverses the control plane network.
- Data plane (inference GPUs) lives in tenant-isolated subnets. Tenants are mapped to dedicated runtime slices (software multi-tenant) with per-tenant network namespaces and iptables-based filters at the sidecar.
- KV cache is per-runtime instance; we never persist cross-tenant KV state. Batching is workload-aware and tenant boundaries are enforced before batching decisions are materialized.

Attachments in this draft: redwood_trust_zones_v2.pdf (annotated diagram), isolation_matrix_20260422.csv (controls map), operator_guardrails_notes.md (short runbook).

I'll send a slightly expanded threat-model bullet list by 4:30p after a quick internal review with Naomi and Grace. If you want a long-form narrative for auditors we can follow up with the SOC packet.

Best —
Michael Grant
Director, Security Solutions
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: RFI: Traffic separation topology and trust zones (final packet)

Alan / Humana team —

Attached is the packet we discussed: an annotated topology PDF, an isolation controls matrix, and a short operator guardrails note. Executive summary and the three most relevant attack vectors (with mitigations) are below. If you'd like we can convert the attachments into an "evidence packet" for your auditors (zip + MD5) and provide pointer links to SOC artifacts.

Executive summary (TL;DR)
- Control plane and data plane are separately provisioned and logically isolated. Runtime networks are tenant-scoped and prevented from accepting cross-tenant flows by enforcement at the sidecar and host-level network namespaces.
- Operator access is ephemeral and audited; we avoid persistent operator access to runtime dataplane hosts.
- Batching and KV caching are per-tenant; no shared in-memory cache across tenant namespaces is permitted.

Top 3 realistic attack paths and mitigations
1) Misconfigured peering or firewall rule allowing data-plane lateral egress between tenant subnets. Mitigation: automated policy-as-code tests in CI, pre-deploy validation hooks, and runtime eBPF probes that detect anomalous cross-tenant flows and open a circuit-breaker.
2) Compromised operator credentials used to pivot from control plane into data plane. Mitigation: control plane is in a separate VPC with strict one-way egress; operator actions to affect data plane require short-lived authorized sessions with multi-party approval and are recorded in immutable audit logs (KMS-backed).
3) Batch coalescing bug where scheduler incorrectly merges requests. Mitigation: scheduler enforces tenant-id provenance checks and rejects batch candidates that do not share tenant id; we have unit tests and chaos checks in canary that simulate mixed-tenant traffic.

Attachments (attached as stubs in this email):
- redwood_trust_zones_v2.pdf (annotated topology, includes legend for control/data plane, operator paths, and egress filters)
- isolation_matrix_20260422.csv (controls matrix mapping resource class -> enforced boundary -> evidence artifacts)
- operator_guardrails_notes.md (short runbook with escalation and rollback steps)

If useful, next steps we can take:
- Prepare a 1-page auditor-friendly evidence sheet (with links to logs and test-run IDs).
- Schedule an architecture walkthrough with your security team (30–45m).

Happy to walk through the diagram live tomorrow morning.

Regards,
Michael Grant
Director, Security Solutions
Redwood Inference
